title: Words opening with p or f gather on paragraph first lines even with each line's first word set aside
statement: In paragraph text, leaving out the first word of every line, certain words that begin with p or f are at least three times as frequent on a paragraph's first line as on its other lines, and more so than when the words of each page are shuffled.
source: A sharper form of F-008, using the positions para_first_line_rest and not_para_first_line_rest (code merged in 15afd1a). Why it is needed: R-011 landed on F-008 with a plain line chain that has a separate opening mark for a paragraph's first line. That text passed F-008 only through the paragraph's first word (F-003 again): with first words set aside its ratio is about 1.5. The manuscript's is not: on the public practice split the ratio is 8.46 on the evaluation pages (839 first-line words counted) and 10.48 on the training pages, both p = 0.005 against 199 within-page shuffles. So the p and f words spread along the whole first line, which a writer who only marks the paragraph's first word does not produce. Other transliterations, practice evaluation pages: Takahashi 8.83, passing. The pinned RF file fails (1.38), and for a reason that is not a disagreement about the text: it carries no paragraph marks, so there a 'first line' is only the top line of a page (198 words counted, 2 of them opening with p or f); the comparison is not measurable on RF, and the same holds, less visibly, for F-003 and F-008. Not evidence of language: an ornamental habit for a paragraph's top line (tall gallows have room there) would do it, and so does the generator behind R-012 to R-016, whose first lines reuse words only from the same line: 4.3 to 7.0 on six local runs (four seeds and two fits on half the public pages), all passing. Registered so that the generator scoreboard separates procedures that know the first line from those that know only the first word. Threshold 3 as in F-008, far below both public values because the count of p and f words off first lines is small (rate about 0.3%) and the ratio is noisy on a sample of pages.
